name: Hana Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, 43, and I help wire and repair homes and small businesses under an experienced electrician. I've got a vocational certificate and ordinary pay for the trade, but I'm still slower and less skilled than the others. My partner drives a bus, we have children aged nine and fourteen, a mortgage and three months of expenses saved. I use AI daily for little study questions, check the answers against my course notes, and like being able to ask the senior about a real job afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful tool doesn't need a grand story behind it. I use AI every day to make little study questions from the terms on my course, then check the answers against the notes. I'd still rather learn to fit the cable neatly than spend lunch arguing about who predicted what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My regular days cover our share of the mortgage and bills, and we've got three months of expenses saved. I'm still junior, but the firm has plenty of small installation jobs where I can work under supervision. In that picture I don't see my wages disappearing, and there are some other firms nearby if I ever need to look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the supervised installation and repair work, and keep checking study answers against the course notes. Starting this week I'd bring one practical question to the senior electrician on Friday instead of collecting a screenful of answers I couldn't use. I'd continue that habit through the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, because ordinary progress in the trade would suit me. I don't need my whole working life transformed next Tuesday. I'd enjoy feeling that this week's practice was making next week's job easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is still hard in the practical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Reading a route on a drawing and seeing how it will fit in an occupied room. I've got a vocational certificate, but I'm slower than the others and still need my work checked. A quiz can help me remember a word; it can't give me the feel of a tool in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the household look like around that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, my partner drives a bus, and our children are nine and fourteen. We've got a mortgage and live on fairly ordinary wages. We can cover the month and save a little, which is why I can say I'm calm without pretending we're rich.

say: I'd keep **useful tools** without needing a dramatic story about AI.
I'd value **practical learning** more than arguments about who predicted the future.
think: Our regular **wages** cover the mortgage and bills, with three months of expenses saved.
I expect continued **supervised work** on the firm's small installations, with some other local firms available.
do: Keep **supervised installations** and repairs through the first year.
Check daily **study answers** against notes and bring one practical question to the senior every Friday.
feel: **Calm**, with ordinary paid work and steady learning making the next few years look manageable.
S0.quote: A quiz can help me remember a word; it can't give me the feel of a tool in my hand.
fieldNote: Her **calm** rests on regular days, covered household bills and a three-month reserve, rather than high skill she does not yet possess.
She separates **daily study tools** from practical competence, retaining course-note checks, senior oversight and an honest account of below-average speed.

steps.text: Keep supervised electrical work and check daily study against notes and senior guidance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say try the better tools, but keep a list of what still needs a person's hands. I'd volunteer to test a way of sorting the checked job photographs, with the firm's permission. I'd want the team to count missed details as carefully as minutes saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry the owner might plan fewer teams if quoting and scheduling become much quicker. A junior who takes longer is easier to leave out than the electrician who checks the whole job. My own paid days could shrink even while the physical installations continue, so being keen on software doesn't make me feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior this month for a four-job trial of the approved AI photo-sorting tool using completed jobs. I'd compare the result with the checked notes before using any draft in a handover. In the first year I'd record my actual paid days monthly and check posted electrical-helper vacancies if the days no longer covered my share of our ordinary bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I want to understand the changes instead of wait for somebody to explain them badly. I enjoy a test with a result I can check. I don't enjoy wondering whether getting quicker means another junior doesn't get a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still report a poor result from a tool you suggested?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, especially if it missed a photograph that showed why we had changed the cable route. I'd rather the senior electrician thought the photo tool was useless than thought I hid a mistake. Curiosity is meant to help the work, not win me a little contest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave if your days were cut once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the reason and look at the household figures first. A single short week isn't the same as a permanent cut, and we have three months saved. I'd look at real adverts before making any decision about the job I already have.

say: I'd test **tools** while listing what still requires physical work.
I'd count **missed details** as well as minutes saved when comparing the results.
think: Faster **scheduling** could mean fewer teams and fewer paid days for a slower junior.
My interest in **software** doesn't remove concern about my own earnings.
do: Request a **four-job trial** now of approved AI photo sorting on completed jobs.
Check every **draft handover** against verified notes before using it in the first year.
Record **paid days** monthly and check posted helper vacancies if earnings no longer cover ordinary bills.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer paid days, while curious about tools that can be tested honestly.
S1.quote: I'd rather the senior electrician thought the photo tool was useless than thought I hid a mistake.
fieldNote: She links **own-income risk** to team allocation rather than claiming thinking software performs the physical installation immediately.
Her **trial** remains approved and checked, while vacancy searches follow actual income evidence instead of assuming every short week means permanent loss.

steps.text: Test approved AI photo sorting on four completed jobs with senior permission and checking
Check posted helper vacancies if reduced days no longer cover ordinary bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my family that thinking AI in 2028 is followed by capable robots around 2031, not on the same morning. I'd say we should use the gap but not call it permanent safety. I'd still ask the children to finish learning rather than treat every lesson as a lost cause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose paid days as a junior, and robots in 2031 could reach the simple hands-on tasks I'm still learning. Three months saved lets us absorb a short setback, but not years without my wage. My partner's driving wage isn't a promise of safety either, so I want an affordable plan rather than another big prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save another 50 a month now by stopping the small online purchases I make when I'm tired. I'd also test a clothes-mending sideline with my existing sewing machine, spending no more than 60 of spare earnings on thread and basic supplies after checking employment terms and the requirements for taking paid work. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep the electrical job and accept at most two mending orders a month, stopping if payments didn't cover costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious because the household could lose part of its living, but not helpless. A small clothes-mending test is something I can stop without losing the house. I wouldn't tell myself sewing is safe forever when your robots can do hands-on work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why clothes mending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've shortened family trousers for years and already own the machine. I'd start with plain hems and repairs I know I can finish, not promise somebody a wedding dress. I'd check whether anyone actually wanted to pay before buying more equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the side work replace your wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on two orders a month, and I wouldn't put that into the mortgage budget. I'd count only money received after costs. The point is to test another way of earning while the electrical wage is still coming in.

say: I'd explain **thinking AI in 2028** and robots around 2031 as separate stages.
I'd use the **gap** without promising permanent safety or dismissing the children's learning.
think: My **junior paid days** could shrink, with later robots reaching the physical tasks I am learning.
Three months saved covers **short setbacks**, not years without wages or guaranteed safety for my partner's work.
do: Save another **50 monthly** now by stopping small impulse purchases.
Test **clothes mending** only after employment and requirements checks, using existing equipment and at most 60 of spare earnings.
Keep the **electrical job** after 2028 and take at most two orders monthly, stopping if receipts fail to cover costs.
feel: **Anxious** about lost household earnings, with some control through a small and stoppable experiment.
S2.quote: A small clothes-mending test is something I can stop without losing the house.
fieldNote: The **mending experiment** uses an existing skill and machine, a fixed spare-earnings cap, required checks and no assumed wage replacement.
She preserves **robot exposure** for the sideline too, recognising that a physical service is not exempt from the scenario's eventual endpoint.

steps.text: Save 50 extra monthly by stopping impulse purchases
Test two monthly mending orders after required checks within a 60 spare-earnings cap
Keep the electrical job after 2028 while checking actual mending costs and receipts
Accept mending orders only while receipts cover costs, using owned equipment and existing skills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets me add a practical skill instead of hoping faster software makes me a better electrician. Thinking AI in 2031 still comes before robots around 2034. I'd want whatever I learn to be useful on real jobs before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own wages can hold over the next few years while I improve under supervision. A three-month cushion and some nearby firms give me time to choose teaching carefully. I'm still uneasy about what customers will pay for our work once robots can do it too, but that doesn't feel like losing next month's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set aside 40 a month from spare spending now for the practical drawing course advertised at the training centre. After four months I'd enrol in the 160 weekend class only if the dates didn't cost me paid shifts and my partner agreed to cover the children. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid supervised repairs and use the completed course on cable routes checked by the senior electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the longer future and keen to get started on something useful. I like having a price, a date and a way to check the result. I wouldn't call the course protection from robots, just a way to do my current work better while I'm earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the class clashed with paid work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for another date rather than spend the wage as well as the fee. The four monthly deposits would stay in the course pot until a workable class existed. I wouldn't assume my partner could rearrange a bus shift either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the teaching had helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the senior whether I could explain a cable route before touching anything, and whether I needed fewer corrections. I'd still have the same vocational certificate unless I earned something else. Passing a weekend class doesn't make me the person signing off the whole installation.

say: I'd use **five years** to add a practical skill that helps on current jobs.
I'd explain **robots around 2034** still follow thinking AI, rather than promise training removes the endpoint.
think: I expect **near-term wages** to hold while I improve, with a three-month cushion and some local firms available.
I remain **uneasy** about what customers will pay once robots can do the hands-on work.
do: Save **40 monthly** now from spare spending for four months towards the drawing course.
Enrol in the **160 weekend class** only without lost paid shifts and with my partner agreeing childcare.
Keep **supervised repairs** after 2031 and use the completed course on senior-checked cable routes.
feel: **Uneasy** about later change, with enthusiasm for practical teaching at a known affordable price.
S3.quote: Passing a weekend class doesn't make me the person signing off the whole installation.
fieldNote: Her **self-funded course** has an explicit four-month saving plan, no lost paid shifts and childcare consent, instead of silently consuming emergency funds.
She retains **junior status** and supervision after the course, using observed corrections rather than assuming a new licence or senior authority.

steps.text: Take the 160 drawing class after saving the fee without lost shifts or unagreed childcare
Keep supervised repairs after 2031 using senior-checked cable routes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives a family time for several sensible changes instead of one enormous bet. I'd keep trying useful tools and get the practical teaching while I'm earning. I'd still be honest with the children that long warning doesn't mean somebody has mapped their whole working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when capable robots followed, so I can't assume I'd be retired. Still, our current wages cover the mortgage and we have three months put aside. Over the next few years I feel secure enough to learn without treating every purchase as an emergency, while leaving the later question open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep normal saving and take the 160 drawing class only after the same four-month fee saving, no lost paid shifts and agreed childcare. I'd review actual paid days and the emergency reserve with my partner every six months. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid electrical work and compare any side-work receipts with costs before committing more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, with curiosity rather than a race in my head. I'd like to enjoy the children at their current ages as well as prepare. I don't need to pretend the whole decade is guaranteed to use it sensibly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change that calm view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A sustained drop in paid days, or either of us needing the reserve to meet normal monthly bills. We'd check actual income, not wait for a prediction to become a headline. My plan has to answer to the bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you avoid doing with the longer warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't borrow for a machine or call my little mending test a replacement career before it paid. I'd keep any experiment inside spare money and the hours we actually had. Being willing to try things isn't the same as needing every trial to grow.

say: I'd use **ten years** for several sensible changes rather than one enormous financial bet.
I'd keep **learning** while admitting nobody can map the children's whole working future.
think: Our **current wages** cover the mortgage, with three months saved and near-term work looking secure.
I'll still need income after **2036**, so present security doesn't mean an assumed retirement or guaranteed decade.
do: Continue **normal saving** and take the drawing class only with the saved fee, protected wages and agreed childcare.
Review **paid days** and the emergency reserve with my partner every six months.
Keep **paid work** after 2036 and check side-work receipts against costs before adding money.
feel: **Calm** about near-term finances, with curiosity and explicit limits on borrowing and business experiments.
S4.quote: My plan has to answer to the bank balance.
fieldNote: Her **calm** concerns the next few years with bills covered; sustained income loss or reserve depletion would change that view.
The **long horizon** does not grant retirement at 53 or turn a small mending trial into assumed replacement earnings.

steps.text: Take drawing class only after saving 160 without lost shifts and with agreed childcare
Keep paid work after 2036 while reviewing actual earnings and side-work costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I could lose paid days as a junior before robots around 2031 reach more of the physical work. Clear paid-hour offers and practical teaching that doesn't cost me my wages would help. I'd also want room for small earning experiments without anyone pretending they already pay the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how the learning fits round children and working shifts. A course place isn't usable if the family has no way to cover the afternoon. I like moving quickly, but I still have to check who is actually free.

headlineQuote: A course place isn't usable if the family has no way to cover the afternoon.
portrait: Hana is **43**, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, typical pay and senior checks despite daily AI-assisted study.
Her **partner drives a bus**; two school-age children and a mortgage share a household with three months of expenses saved.
She responds to **short deadlines** with extra saving and a limited mending test, never assuming that physical side work escapes robots.
Longer horizons allow **self-funded drawing teaching** only with a saved fee, protected paid shifts and her partner's agreement on childcare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens junior paid days before capable robots follow around 2031, leaving less time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **paid-hour offers** and practical teaching without lost wages would help her keep earning while learning.
Room for **small experiments** would help if actual receipts are kept separate from hoped-for mortgage income.
